newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu to head home Friday, rebel support growing.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to head home Friday, rebel support growing.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko heads home on Friday after fresh cancer treatment in search of a political solution to Zaire's civil war in the face of growing popular support for rebel leader Laurent Kabila.

As the rebels insisted that only face-to-face talks between Kabila and Mobutu would halt the fighting, France advised its nationals to leave Zaire and sent troops and aircrafts to nearby Congo and Gabon to protect them if need be.

Zaire's main opposition group, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) of veteran radical Etienne Tshisekedi, said it shared Kabila's aim of toppling Mobutu and had sent envoys to talk to him.
Mobutu's son Nzanga said his father did not rule out talks with the rebels but that had to be done in agreement with the government and the parliament.
"He is going to the capital tomorrow. His intention is to find a solution to the present crisis in consultation with parliament, the government and the military high command."
Prime Minister Kenga wa Dondo, under fire for his handling of the war, returned home on Thursday from Kenya, where he backed a regional call for a truce and talks.
While he was away, the transitional parliament voted to sack him in a vote rejected by his and Mobutu supporters as invalid.
"He said when he arrived at midday that he is still prime minister until further notice," one source close to Kengo said.
In Lubumbashi, the leader of the biggest party in Zaire's autonomy-hungry mining province of Shaba said nothing would stop Kabila's rebels taking the province if the war went on.
Kyungu wa Kumwanza, Shaba's suspended governor, called on Mobutu to meet Kabila for talks but said they must also include regional leaders such as himself.
"The truth is, all the people here are waiting eagerly for Mr Kabila. They see him as a saviour," Kyungu said.
Kenya's foreign minister, Laurent Kabila, said U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would fly on Friday to rebel-held eastern Zaire to meet Kabila and press him to support a ceasefire.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in Cape Town that if a ceasefire could be brokered in Zaire the Security Council might send troops to bolster the peace.

The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute about Zairean nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority, who form the core of Kabila's fighting force. An alliance of anti-Mobutu groups rallied around the cause.

Kabila's popularity has increased dramatically as his forces have notched up victory after victory. Residents of Kinshasa's poor districts, Tshisekedi's power base, openly welcome the prospect of his arrival in the capital.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland in August and has spent most of his time in Europe since then, left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh treatment.
He will return to fresh squabbling among Zaire's political family as rival leaders jockey for position -- keen not to lose out in any deal with Kabila.

A national conference elected Tshisekedi prime minister in 1992 but Mobutu sacked him a year later in favour of one of his own appointees. Tshisekedi has never accepted Kengo's appointment in 1994 as a later compromise candidate.
"Mr Tshisekedi must immediately be reinstated as prime minister," UDPS secretary-general Adrien Phongo said.
